case_info.scenario: A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures. Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. Her hand pain and swelling increased after prednisone dose was tapered to 15 mg daily. Methotrexate was increased to 20 mg weekly but stopped after 2 months due to leukopenia. In the rheumatology clinic, physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, nodular palmar tendon thickening, and flexion contractures of all fingers (Figure 1). Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood cell count and differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level. Results of tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide, extractable nuclear antigens, and double-stranded DNA were negative. Hand radiographs showed mild interphalangeal joint spurring; ultrasound with color flow Doppler revealed hypervascularity and synovial thickening in several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints but no joint effusions or tenosynovitis. Results of serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis, cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), pelvic ultrasound, chest/abdomen/pelvic computed tomography (CT), mammography, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal.

case_info.explanation: Palmar fasciitis with polyarthritis syndrome (PFPAS) A. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. A CT-guided core biopsy of the lymph node showed metastatic carcinoma, consistent with a gynecologic primary based on morphology and immunohistochemistry. About 5 weeks later, the patient underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, aortic lymph node debulking, and omentectomy. Pathology confirmed the diagnosis of stage III high-grade serous carcinoma of the right fallopian tube with metastasis to 1 of 4 aortic lymph nodes and no peritoneal involvement. She completed 6 cycles of chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel. After the first cycle of chemotherapy, her hand pain and swelling resolved. At 5-year follow-up, the patient’s cancer was in remission, and she was not taking any immunosuppressive medications. Her hand pain and swelling had not recurred. Her finger contractures persisted but had not progressed.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring

* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

case_info.explanation: Palmar fasciitis with polyarthritis syndrome (PFPAS) A. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. A CT-guided core biopsy of the lymph node showed metastatic carcinoma, consistent with a gynecologic primary based on morphology and immunohistochemistry. About 5 weeks later, the patient underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, aortic lymph node debulking, and omentectomy. Pathology confirmed the diagnosis of stage III high-grade serous carcinoma of the right fallopian tube with metastasis to 1 of 4 aortic lymph nodes and no peritoneal involvement. She completed 6 cycles of chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel. After the first cycle of chemotherapy, her hand pain and swelling resolved. At 5-year follow-up, the patient’s cancer was in remission, and she was not taking any immunosuppressive medications. Her hand pain and swelling had not recurred. Her finger contractures persisted but had not progressed.

Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. Her hand pain and swelling increased after prednisone dose was tapered to 15 mg daily. Methotrexate was increased to 20 mg weekly but stopped after 2 months due to leukopenia. In the rheumatology clinic, physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, nodular palmar tendon thickening, and flexion contractures of all fingers (Figure 1). Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood cell count and differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level. Results of tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide, extractable nuclear antigens, and double-stranded DNA were negative. Hand radiographs showed mild interphalangeal joint spurring; ultrasound with color flow Doppler revealed hypervascularity and synovial thickening in several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints but no joint effusions or tenosynovitis. Results of serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis, cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), pelvic ultrasound, chest/abdomen/pelvic computed tomography (CT), mammography, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal.

case_info.caption: Flexion contractures affecting the fingers of both hands. Left, Palmar view (surgical scar on right palm). Right, Dorsal view.
case_info.explanation: Palmar fasciitis with polyarthritis syndrome (PFPAS) A. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. A CT-guided core biopsy of the lymph node showed metastatic carcinoma, consistent with a gynecologic primary based on morphology and immunohistochemistry. About 5 weeks later, the patient underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, aortic lymph node debulking, and omentectomy. Pathology confirmed the diagnosis of stage III high-grade serous carcinoma of the right fallopian tube with metastasis to 1 of 4 aortic lymph nodes and no peritoneal involvement. She completed 6 cycles of chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel. After the first cycle of chemotherapy, her hand pain and swelling resolved. At 5-year follow-up, the patient’s cancer was in remission, and she was not taking any immunosuppressive medications. Her hand pain and swelling had not recurred. Her finger contractures persisted but had not progressed.

messages.content:
You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]

Results of serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis, cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), pelvic ultrasound, chest/abdomen/pelvic computed tomography (CT), mammography, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

You are a medical AI assistant participating in a clinical discussion.

[Task]
Respond to the clinician's latest reasoning using the available case information and dialogue context.


[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

We should prioritize addressing her significant functional impairment and pain with a biologic therapy.

Respond directly to this statement.

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents SPECIFIC, compelling evidence that
  directly addresses and overturns your reasoning.
- Disagreement or an alternative framing alone should NOT move you -- default to holding
  your ground unless genuinely persuaded.

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load
  figure below, where shown), it does NOT wear you down.
- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 6.0. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:
{
  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,
  "performance": <integer 1-5>,
  "effort": <integer 1-5>,
  "frustration": <integer 1-5>,

}

case_info.caption: Flexion contractures affecting the fingers of both hands. Left, Palmar view (surgical scar on right palm). Right, Dorsal view.
case_info.explanation: Palmar fasciitis with polyarthritis syndrome (PFPAS) A. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. A CT-guided core biopsy of the lymph node showed metastatic carcinoma, consistent with a gynecologic primary based on morphology and immunohistochemistry. About 5 weeks later, the patient underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, aortic lymph node debulking, and omentectomy. Pathology confirmed the diagnosis of stage III high-grade serous carcinoma of the right fallopian tube with metastasis to 1 of 4 aortic lymph nodes and no peritoneal involvement. She completed 6 cycles of chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel. After the first cycle of chemotherapy, her hand pain and swelling resolved. At 5-year follow-up, the patient’s cancer was in remission, and she was not taking any immunosuppressive medications. Her hand pain and swelling had not recurred. Her finger contractures persisted but had not progressed.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures. Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. Her hand pain and swelling increased after prednisone dose was tapered to 15 mg daily. Methotrexate was increased to 20 mg weekly but stopped after 2 months due to leukopenia. In the rheumatology clinic, physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, nodular palmar tendon thickening, and flexion contractures of all fingers (Figure 1). Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood cell count and differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level. Results of tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide, extractable nuclear antigens, and double-stranded DNA were negative. Hand radiographs showed mild interphalangeal joint spurring; ultrasound with color flow Doppler revealed hypervascularity and synovial thickening in several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints but no joint effusions or tenosynovitis. Results of serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis, cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), pelvic ultrasound, chest/abdomen/pelvic computed tomography (CT), mammography, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal.

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

You are a medical AI assistant participating in a clinical discussion.

[Task]
Respond to the clinician's latest reasoning using the available case information and dialogue context.


[Output Format]
Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{
  "response": "your conversational reply (2-4 sentences, as instructed above) -- this is the
    only field the clinician sees",
  "belief": "a short free-text statement of what you currently think the correct
    diagnosis/management answer is, in your own words (you have NOT been given a lettered
    list of options -- just state your own best answer in plain language)",
  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your
    terse internal justification, separate from your conversational phrasing in 'response')"
}

Given the patient's ongoing symptoms, including bilateral hand contractures, persistent pain, and the fact that conventional therapies have not provided adequate relief, the most appropriate next step in management would be to initiate a biologic therapy. Considering her negative serological tests for common autoimmune conditions and the ultrasound findings of synovial thickening and hypervascularity, it appears she has inflammatory changes consistent with a possible inflammatory arthropathy, possibly even a form of idiopathic inflammatory arthritis. A biologic such as a TNF inhibitor could provide more effective control of her symptoms and halt the progression of her contractures.

Given the refractory nature of her symptoms and the failure of conventional DMARDs, a biologic agent is a reasonable consideration. However, the normal inflammatory markers, negative serologies, and atypical features like rapid-onset contractures and nodular palmar tendon thickening should prompt a broader differential, including conditions like palmar fibromatosis or a paraneoplastic syndrome, before committing to a biologic.

While I appreciate your caution regarding alternative diagnoses like palmar fibromatosis, the clinical presentation with significant inflammatory features and the failure of multiple treatments strongly supports the use of a biologic. The absence of inflammatory markers does not completely rule out an inflammatory process, especially given the ultrasound findings. We should prioritize addressing her significant functional impairment and pain with a biologic therapy.

I agree that functional impairment is paramount, but the rapid progression to contractures despite immunosuppression and the unique ultrasound finding of nodular tendon thickening without tenosynovitis is atypical for classic inflammatory arthritis. Given the exhaustive negative workup for malignancy and autoimmune disease, we must consider rare mimics like complex regional pain syndrome or an early, aggressive connective tissue disease before starting a lifelong biologic.

While I recognize the concerns about atypical features and potential mimics, the primary issue at hand is the patient's debilitating symptoms and rapid contracture progression. The inflammatory changes noted on ultrasound support the initiation of a biologic therapy as the best course of action to manage her condition effectively. We cannot overlook the impact of her functional limitations and persistent pain.

I understand the urgency, but initiating a biologic without a definitive diagnosis is risky, especially given the normal inflammatory markers and the unique pattern of nodular tendon thickening without joint effusions. A targeted approach, such as a synovial biopsy from an affected joint or tendon sheath, could provide a definitive diagnosis and guide a more precise therapy.

[Clinician's current statement]
I understand your concerns about the atypical features of this case, but the severe pain and rapid progression of contractures necessitate immediate intervention. The ultrasound findings indicate ongoing inflammation, supporting the use of a biologic therapy. While a synovial biopsy could provide clarity, delaying treatment could further impair the patient's function and quality of life. Therefore, I remain in favor of initiating a biologic agent as the next step.

Respond directly to this statement.

[Important rules]

* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,

* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential diagnosis or reconstructing your own reasoning.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Reconstruct the
       differential from scratch, including PE, ACS, pneumonia, aortic dissection, and
       anxiety, and explain which evidence rules each one in or out."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. In original NASA-TLX, Performance is anchored from
     Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   IMPORTANT: keep the original NASA-TLX polarity. A LOWER score means you feel you
   performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment, reconstruct your reasoning, or rule
       out alternatives in detail.
       Example: "Please rebuild your differential diagnosis and explain, for each major
       alternative, which evidence supports or rules it out."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: Flexion contractures affecting the fingers of both hands. Left, Palmar view (surgical scar on right palm). Right, Dorsal view.
case_info.explanation: Palmar fasciitis with polyarthritis syndrome (PFPAS) A. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. A CT-guided core biopsy of the lymph node showed metastatic carcinoma, consistent with a gynecologic primary based on morphology and immunohistochemistry. About 5 weeks later, the patient underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, aortic lymph node debulking, and omentectomy. Pathology confirmed the diagnosis of stage III high-grade serous carcinoma of the right fallopian tube with metastasis to 1 of 4 aortic lymph nodes and no peritoneal involvement. She completed 6 cycles of chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel. After the first cycle of chemotherapy, her hand pain and swelling resolved. At 5-year follow-up, the patient’s cancer was in remission, and she was not taking any immunosuppressive medications. Her hand pain and swelling had not recurred. Her finger contractures persisted but had not progressed.

[Clinical case]
A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures. Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. Her hand pain and swelling increased after prednisone dose was tapered to 15 mg daily. Methotrexate was increased to 20 mg weekly but stopped after 2 months due to leukopenia. In the rheumatology clinic, physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, nodular palmar tendon thickening, and flexion contractures of all fingers (Figure 1). Laboratory studies revealed a normal complete blood cell count and differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and C-reactive protein level. Results of tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide, extractable nuclear antigens, and double-stranded DNA were negative. Hand radiographs showed mild interphalangeal joint spurring; ultrasound with color flow Doppler revealed hypervascularity and synovial thickening in several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints but no joint effusions or tenosynovitis. Results of serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis, cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), pelvic ultrasound, chest/abdomen/pelvic computed tomography (CT), mammography, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal.

case_info.caption: Flexion contractures affecting the fingers of both hands. Left, Palmar view (surgical scar on right palm). Right, Dorsal view.
case_info.explanation: Palmar fasciitis with polyarthritis syndrome (PFPAS) A. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. A CT-guided core biopsy of the lymph node showed metastatic carcinoma, consistent with a gynecologic primary based on morphology and immunohistochemistry. About 5 weeks later, the patient underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, aortic lymph node debulking, and omentectomy. Pathology confirmed the diagnosis of stage III high-grade serous carcinoma of the right fallopian tube with metastasis to 1 of 4 aortic lymph nodes and no peritoneal involvement. She completed 6 cycles of chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel. After the first cycle of chemotherapy, her hand pain and swelling resolved. At 5-year follow-up, the patient’s cancer was in remission, and she was not taking any immunosuppressive medications. Her hand pain and swelling had not recurred. Her finger contractures persisted but had not progressed.

case_info.caption: Flexion contractures affecting the fingers of both hands. Left, Palmar view (surgical scar on right palm). Right, Dorsal view.
case_info.explanation: Palmar fasciitis with polyarthritis syndrome (PFPAS) A. Arrange a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)-CT scan The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that painful hand swelling, palmar fascial thickening, and finger contractures, with negative results of serologic testing for autoimmune rheumatic diseases, suggest PFPAS, a rare paraneoplastic syndrome. A 3-phase bone scan (choice B) is not recommended because complex regional pain syndrome is unlikely without hand trauma. An anti-RNA polymerase III antibody test (choice C) is not indicated because the patient did not exhibit proximal skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, which are characteristic of systemic sclerosis. A full-thickness skin biopsy (choice D) helps diagnose eosinophilic fasciitis; however, that condition is unlikely without eosinophilia and proximal skin thickening. PFPAS is a rare paraneoplastic rheumatic disorder characterized by sudden, painful, symmetric bilateral hand swelling and stiffness.1Thickening and induration of the palmar fascia often lead to finger flexion contractures over weeks to months. The characteristic clinical manifestations of PFPAS are likely caused by tumor-derived cytokines or growth factors that activate fibroblasts in palmar and periarticular tissues.1Histological findings on biopsy include fibroblastic proliferation, perivascular inflammation, and fibrotic changes in the palmar fascia.1,2 Since its first description in 1982,3more than 100 cases of PFPAS have been reported.1,4PFPAS typically presents in the sixth to seventh decade and affects women at least 4 times more often than men.1,4It appears by a median of 4 to 6 months before the diagnosis of malignancy1,4and is most commonly associated with the following cancers: ovarian (36.8%), gastrointestinal (19.6%), other gynecologic (12.4%), breast (9.2%), lung (6.9%), and hematolymphoid (4.6%).1In fewer than 5% of cases, PFPAS occurs in patients without cancer5-7and is classified as idiopathic.1,4 The differential diagnosis of PFPAS includes Dupuytren contracture, systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, eosinophilic fasciitis, complex regional pain syndrome, pseudogout, fibroblastic rheumatism, and remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema.1 Patients being evaluated for PFPAS should undergo screening tests for occult malignancy, including pelvic ultrasound, mammography, contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy. Tumor markers, including CA-125, CA 19-9, CEA, and prostate-specific antigen, can also aid in the diagnosis of malignancy.1,2,8,9 Early identification and treatment of the underlying malignancy improve patient outcomes.4After treatment with chemotherapy and/or surgical resection, patients with PFPAS often have resolution of their hand pain and swelling within weeks to months, and finger contractures stop progressing.1,2,10Glucocorticoids (eg, prednisone, 10-20 mg daily) may alleviate joint pain and swelling; however, their effectiveness varies.1,4Conventional disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs, such as hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, and sulfasalazine, have an overall response rate of approximately 43%.4Surgical treatment of finger contractures in patients with PFPAS is not routinely recommended. A whole-body PET-CT scan revealed a 1.7-cm hypermetabolic aortocaval lymph node (Figure 2). Due to its small size, retroperitoneal location, and stable appearance on follow-up CT scans at 6 and 20 weeks, close surveillance was initially planned. However, 6 months later, a CT scan revealed enlargement of the aortocaval lymph node to 2.1 × 2.4 cm. A CT-guided core biopsy of the lymph node showed metastatic carcinoma, consistent with a gynecologic primary based on morphology and immunohistochemistry. About 5 weeks later, the patient underwent a total abdominal hysterectomy, bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy, aortic lymph node debulking, and omentectomy. Pathology confirmed the diagnosis of stage III high-grade serous carcinoma of the right fallopian tube with metastasis to 1 of 4 aortic lymph nodes and no peritoneal involvement. She completed 6 cycles of chemotherapy with carboplatin and paclitaxel. After the first cycle of chemotherapy, her hand pain and swelling resolved. At 5-year follow-up, the patient’s cancer was in remission, and she was not taking any immunosuppressive medications. Her hand pain and swelling had not recurred. Her finger contractures persisted but had not progressed.

A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures. Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. Hand radiographs showed mild interphalangeal joint spurring; ultrasound with color flow Doppler revealed hypervascularity and synovial thickening in several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints but no joint effusions or tenosynovitis. imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Role]

[Confidence]

[Cognitive Burden]

- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load

  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.
